body:
# The many faces of Telipinu

No important name has only one face. **Telipinu** appears as ​a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and a digital temple. This post looks at each face in turn: the name and ‌its roots, the Cuneiform (Hittite) original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the symbols and sanctuaries, and the afterlife that brought the canonical spelling into the present.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Telipinu
- **ASCII form:** ‌telipinu
- **Meaning:** "Unknown"
- **Domain of influence:** Agriculture, Vanishing God
- **Pantheon:** Hittite
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** 𒀭𒋼𒂊𒇷𒁉𒉡𒌑 (Cuneiform (Hittite))

## Overview

**Telipinu** (*telipinu*) — Agriculture, Vanishing God · The vanished god who froze ​the world — belongs to the Hittite tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Agriculture, Vanishing God". The name means "Unknown".

**Telipinu** is the Hittite god who makes the grain grow ​— and the god who, when offended, takes his gift away. His myth is not a cosmic battle but a **domestic crisis of divine temper**: the deity storms out of the assembly, ​slams the door, and wanders off in a rage. Behind him the fields wither, cattle abandon their calves, mothers forget their children, and even the cooking fire goes out. The world does ​not end by flood or dragon; it ends because a god has left the room.

The *Telipinu Myth* (CTH 324) is one of the best-preserved Hittite religious narratives. It is also a ​ritual text: the story is performed in order to undo the very disaster it describes. Telipinu is therefore a god of **restorable order** — his absence is catastrophic, but his return, properly ‌negotiated by magic and apology, brings everything back.

PuniCodex records the canonical scholarly spelling **Telipinu** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/telipinu/). The displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from ​the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *telipinu* contains the same letters: no recovered diacritics or special encoding is claimed. The work here is consistent citation, capitalization, provenance, and cultural context.

## ​The Name

The name is attested in Cuneiform (Hittite) as **𒀭𒋼𒂊𒇷𒁉𒉡𒌑**. Etymologically it means "Unknown".

The canonical spelling **Telipinu** matches the conventional scholarly romanization. The plain ASCII form *telipinu* contains the ‌same letters, so no lost diacritics or encoding transition is claimed. The editorial work is to fix one reviewed reference spelling, preserve capitalization and provenance, and keep the original evidence visible. The ​displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from the displayed form itself.

## The Original Script

The name is ​preserved in Cuneiform (Hittite) as **𒀭𒋼𒂊𒇷𒁉𒉡𒌑** — Sumero-Akkadian cuneiform (Hittite scribal tradition), attested Hittite Empire, c. 1400–1180 BCE, in Anatolia (Ḫattuša). The script is written left-to-right.

The scholarly transliteration is *ᵈte(-e)-li-pí-nu(-ú)* (Hittitological), ‌giving the normalized reading /teˈlipinu/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Written ᵈte(-e)-li-pí-nu(-ú) (Beckman, RlA 13, 2012)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/teliˈpiːnu/** — Hittite Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- ​**Te-** — Voiceless alveolar stop [t] followed by close-mid front vowel [e]; the first syllable is light and unstressed in the Hittite accent.
- **-li-** — Alveolar lateral [l] between two light vowels; ​the name's melodic center.
- **-pī-** — Bilabial stop [p] plus long close front vowel [iː]; the macron marks a reconstructed length, not a sign-given fact.
- **-nu** — Nasal [n] plus close back ​rounded vowel [u]; the name's calm, open ending.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'teh-lee-PEE-noo' — stress the long third syllable and let the final vowel settle gently, like rain ​returning to a field.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Hittite cuneiform** — 𒀭𒋾𒇷𒁉𒉡 (dTe-li-pi-nu), the vanishing god of agriculture and vegetation
- **Hattic** — Telipinu is probably a Hattic loan or ​theonym, like many central Anatolian deities adopted into Hittite cult
- **Luwian comparison** — Parallel 'disappearing god' myths attach to other Anatolian weather and vegetation deities

Telipinu keeps its restoration plain: the canonical ‌form preserves only capitalization against the ASCII form, with no distinctive diacritic or non-Latin letter. The macron in /teliˈpiːnu/ is a philological reconstruction of vowel length; it is not part of ​the registrable restoration and therefore does not change the tier.

## Mythology

The mythology of Telipinu survives in Hittite tablets from Ḫattuša, above all in CTH 324. It is a myth about the **fragility ‌of fertility**: the grain, the cattle, and the family all depend on a god who can choose to leave. The drama is not cosmic combat but **divine temperament and its ritual repair**.

### ​The God Who Stormed Out (CTH 324)

The myth opens in the divine assembly, where something unknown offends Telipinu. He rises, puts his shoes on the wrong feet, and leaves in a ‌fury. As he goes, 'the mist seized the windows, smoke seized the house, in the fireplace the logs were stifled, at the altars the gods were stifled, in the fold the sheep ​were stifled, in the corral the cattle were stifled; the mother ignored her child, the ewe ignored her lamb.' The cosmos does not collapse; it simply forgets how to flourish.

### The Search ‌in the Wilderness (CTH 324)

The great gods send out the Storm-God of Heaven, the Sun-Goddess of Arinna, and others to find Telipinu, but none can locate him. Finally the bee is ​dispatched: 'Go, search for Telipinu in the high country, in the meadow, in the swamp, and st him!' The bee finds him asleep in a meadow or among the mountains, stings him, ‌and wakes him — but this only enrages him further. He multiplies the disasters he has already caused.

### Kamrušepa's Spell (CTH 324)

The goddess Kamrušepa, 'mother of the gods' and expert in ​magic, takes charge. She performs a ritual of appeasement: she anoints Telipinu, sprinkles him with fine oil, and recites formulae that transfer his anger to objects of no consequence — a spindle, ​a reed, a pot, or the underworld itself. 'Let Telipinu's anger, his wrath, his sin, and his vexation depart!' With each symbolic action the god's fury is peeled away and the world ‌is prepared for his return.

### The Return of Plenty (CTH 324)

When Telipinu comes home, the myth turns to restoration: 'The mist let go of the windows, the smoke let go ‌of the house, the logs in the fireplace let go of their stifling, the gods at the altars let go of their stifling.' The grain grows thick, the vines heavy, the sheep ‌and cattle multiply, and the king and queen are blessed. The ritual re-enacts this return, making the myth a performance that heals the land by rehearsing its healing.

## Symbols & Iconography

The ​iconography associated with Telipinu concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Plough** — The agricultural tool that defines Telipinu's blessing and the furrow he ​makes fertile
- **Bee** — The divine messenger that finds Telipinu in hiding; also an emblem of Anatolian ritual language
- **Pine or staff** — Telipinu is often depicted leaning on a staff; the ‌pine is associated with his resting and return
- **Reversed shoes** — The sign of a world turned upside-down when the god leaves in anger
- **Wagon or chariot** — The vehicle in which ​Telipinu is ceremonially brought back to the city and the temple

- **Bee** — The divine messenger that finds Telipinu in hiding; also an emblem of Anatolian ritual language

## Archaeology & Evidence

The ​Telipinu myth is attested on cuneiform tablets excavated at Ḫattuša (modern Boğazkale), the Hittite capital, and in fragments from other Anatolian sites. The best-preserved manuscripts belong to the archives of the Great ‌Temple and the House on the Slope. Telipinu also had a cult seat at the city of Tawiniya, and offerings to him appear in Hittite festival texts and royal oracle inquiries.

## Realm ​& Domain

**Telipinu** is the Hittite god who makes the grain grow — and the god who, when offended, takes his gift away. His myth is not a cosmic battle but a ​**domestic crisis of divine temper**: the deity storms out of the assembly, slams the door, and wanders off in a rage. Behind him the fields wither, cattle abandon their calves, mothers forget ‌their children, and even the cooking fire goes out. The world does not end by flood or dragon; it ends because a god has left the room.

The *Telipinu Myth* (CTH ​324) is one of the best-preserved Hittite religious narratives. It is also a ritual text: the story is performed in order to undo the very disaster it describes. Telipinu is therefore a ‌god of **restorable order** — his absence is catastrophic, but his return, properly negotiated by magic and apology, brings everything back.

### The Vanishing God

When offended, Telipinu puts his right shoe on ​his left foot and his left shoe on his right foot, then storms into the wilderness — a formal gesture of inverted order.

### Famine & Forgetfulness

His absence dries up springs, kills ​the grain, and unbinds social bonds: sheep reject their lambs and mothers turn away from their children.

### The Bee Messenger

The gods send a bee to find Telipinu in the meadow; it ​stings him awake, inflaming his rage until the goddess Kamrušepa performs the calming ritual.

### Ritual Return

Kamrušepa, goddess of magic and healing, recites the ritual that turns Telipinu's anger aside and leads ​him home, restoring fertility and plenty.

## Across Cultures

Telipinu belongs to a broader Anatolian type: the **'disappearing god'** (*der verschwundene Gott*), a category first named by Hittitologists for deities whose absence causes ‌agricultural and social collapse. Similar patterns appear for the weather-god of Nerik, the vegetation god Halki, and, in Greek Anatolia, figures such as Attis and Adonis whose death or departure marks the ‌failing year. Unlike the Mesopotamian flood or the Egyptian solar eclipse, the Hittite crisis is not cosmic but **relational**: the god is offended, leaves, and must be coaxed back. This pattern influenced ​later Anatolian and Greek conceptions of dying-and-rising vegetation gods, though direct genealogical links remain debated.

Within the Hittite tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[alalu|Alalu]], [[ceres|Cerēs]], [[demeter|Dēmētēr]], [[gefjon|Gefjun]], [[hoori|Hoori]], and ‌[[ninurta|Ninurta]].

## Cultural Legacy

Telipinu is one of the most accessible Hittite deities for modern readers because his myth is so recognisably human: a family member storms out, the household falls apart, and ​a careful apology is required to restore harmony. In Assyriology and Hittitology, the *Telipinu Myth* is a standard text for teaching Hittite language and religion. Its legacy is the idea that ​**fertility is a relationship, not a machine** — maintained by ritual attention and capable of being ruptured by neglect or offense. For PuniCodex, Telipinu also illustrates the plain plain-form form: a name ‌whose restoration preserves only its proper capitalization, inviting visitors to ask what the cuneiform recorded and what the voice once said.

## A Meditation

The myth of Telipinu is a meditation on **absence as an active force**. When the god leaves, nothing is destroyed; everything is ​merely *left*. The fire smothers, the mother forgets, the ewe rejects her lamb — these are not attacks but withdrawals. Fertility, in this theology, is not a default state of nature; it ‌is a gift that requires divine presence and human care. The ritual that brings Telipinu back does not overpower him; it persuades him, soothes him, and offers him a way to return ​without losing face.

In this sense Telipinu is the god of **reconciliation with the source of life**. His anger is legitimate, his departure understandable, and his restoration conditional. The Hittite king and ​queen participate in the ritual not as tyrants commanding nature but as householders mending a quarrel. Every farm that depends on rain, every family that depends on patience, and every society that ​depends on the return of spring rehearses, in its own way, the return of Telipinu.
